title: Stage Capabilities: Upload Tool
summary: Adversaries stage tooling on infrastructure they control or have compromised so it can be pulled down later, mid intrusion, without ever touching the target beforehand. Unlike malware, these are legitimate utilities that keep their original file names and vendor signatures, which is exactly why they survive reputation checks. The upload usually travels over ordinary web protocols to a rented virtual private server, a hijacked content management system, a public code repository, or a platform as a service host. Defenders rarely see the upload at all, because it happens on third party infrastructure outside their visibility. The observable signal comes later: an endpoint or server fetching an unsigned or unusual executable from an unfamiliar external address, or a file appearing in a temporary directory shortly before execution. Telling this apart from normal administration means checking whether the source host is an approved software distribution point and whether many machines pulled the same binary in a short window.

beginner.definition: Uploading a tool means putting a program on a server so you can fetch it later. The program is not malware by itself. It is a normal utility that many people use, such as a remote administration tool. The attacker stores it somewhere they can reach from inside your network. This is one part of a wider idea called staging capabilities, where an attacker prepares everything before the attack starts.
beginner.whyItMatters: If nobody watches for file downloads, an attacker can bring in tools whenever they like. These tools look normal, so antivirus may not complain about them. That gives the attacker a way to run commands and move between your machines. Blocking unknown download sources makes this much harder.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a place to store the tool, often a rented server or a hacked website.
They upload the utility there, sometimes keeping its original name and signature intact.
Later they connect from inside your network and download the file over normal web traffic.
The file may land in a temporary folder, a user profile, or a shared drive.
A script or a person then runs the tool to control other machines in your network.
Because the upload happened outside your network, only the download is visible to you.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat where every resident has a key to the front door. A visitor cannot get a key, so instead they leave a toolbox in the corridor cupboard during a party, when nobody is checking. Days later they come back as a guest, open the cupboard, and use your own screwdriver to take the door off its hinges. The toolbox was never hidden and never looked dangerous. The moment that mattered was the quiet visit when it was placed there, and the second visit when it was collected.
takeaways: Attackers store their tools outside your network, then download them when needed.
These tools are legitimate software, so a clean virus scan proves very little.
Watch which external sites your machines download programs from.

objectives: Explain why staging a legitimate tool is different from staging malware.
Describe the places attackers commonly store tools before an intrusion.
Identify the download event that reveals staging after the fact.
Explain how to tell an approved software source from an unfamiliar one.
Summarise what a defender can and cannot see when a tool is staged externally.
